error_modes.label: Continuous airspace check while leading the formation

texts.0: SP, due to an inside-cockpit fixation on the navigation display while leading, did not continuously check the airspace for the period he/she was in charge of the formation, leaving the sector ahead and above unscanned through the turn to initial. The lookout lapse persisted into the landing pattern, where the requirement is highest, and the IP had to take the aircraft and direct the deconfliction turn. The outside scan was re-established only after the IP intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to prolonged head-down time on the fuel and engine indications, did not maintain a continuous check of the airspace while leading, and the outside scan stopped for several seconds at a time on downwind. The pattern lookout was restored only after two verbal prompts from the IP, and the delay left the base turn started without a clearing check. No control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to task loading from the formation position calls, allowed the outside scan to break during the level-off, and for a short period the airspace ahead of the formation went unchecked. SP recognized the lapse and re-established the continuous check before entering the pattern, without any prompting. Separation from the reported traffic was never in question.
texts.3: SP continuously checked the airspace for the full period he/she was in charge of the formation, interrupting the outside scan only briefly for essential cockpit references. The lookout was tightened in the landing pattern as required and every leg was entered with the airspace checked. No prompting was necessary at any stage.
texts.4: SP kept an uninterrupted airspace check throughout the lead period, integrating the required cockpit references without any measurable break in the outside scan. In the landing pattern the coverage was extended to the extended centerline and to the opposite base with time in hand. Deviations from the required lookout were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP checked the airspace continuously and within standard for the whole lead period, but the coverage was consistently weighted to the front quadrant and the high check was thin on the crosswind leg. Head-down periods lengthened noticeably as the sortie progressed. The standard was met on this sortie; SP is expected to even out the scan pattern and hold the same coverage late in the profile.

error_modes.label: Timely detection of nearby aircraft and maintenance of proper separation

texts.0: SP, due to a scan restricted to the formation and to the ground references, did not locate the nearby aircraft in time, and the traffic was called first by the IP inside the turn. Proper separation was not maintained and the IP took the aircraft to open the geometry. Post-flight reconstruction showed the target had been in the unscanned sector for the whole of its approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow sector-by-sector scan pattern, located the converging aircraft late and did not initiate the separation manoeuvre on his/her own assessment. The turn away was flown only after the IP called the traffic and directed the correction, and separation ended at the minimum acceptable margin. No control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the wingman's position during the rejoin, detected the crossing traffic later than the available cues allowed, but located it without prompting and adjusted heading in time. Separation was reduced from the planned margin yet remained comfortable throughout. The correction was unaided and early enough to avoid any abrupt manoeuvring.
texts.3: SP located nearby flying aircraft in good time in every case, using a full sector scan, and maintained proper separation with small planned heading adjustments. Traffic was called before the IP had any reason to intervene. Separation was never allowed to compress.
texts.4: SP located all nearby aircraft at long range, including a target crossing well above the formation, and maintained separation with early minimal adjustments that preserved the profile. Traffic assessments were passed to the wingman with accurate position and relative motion. Any shortfall in timeliness was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP located nearby aircraft within standard, but detection was consistently at close range rather than early, so separation was preserved through larger corrections than necessary. The pattern was most evident against traffic on a low-relative-motion track. Performance met the standard; SP is expected to detect earlier and correct sooner.

error_modes.label: Conception of active and potential hazards and regulation of flight parameters

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the planned profile after the build-up over the working area had already been observed, did not conceive the developing hazard and did not regulate the flight parameters to avoid it. The formation was held on the briefed heading and altitude until the IP took the aircraft and turned the flight clear. The hazard had been visible and reportable well before that point.
texts.1: SP, due to continuation bias after the conditions at the recovery point had deteriorated, treated the hazard as a present problem rather than a potential one and did not adjust altitude or heading on his/her own initiative. The avoidance turn and descent were flown after repeated verbal direction from the IP, and the margin at the moment of correction was the minimum acceptable. Control of the aircraft remained with SP.
texts.2: SP, due to continuation bias in holding the briefed track, was late in conceiving the potential conflict with traffic recovering from the adjacent area, but reassessed the situation without prompting and regulated speed and heading to open the geometry. The avoidance was flown early enough to keep the profile intact. No direction from the IP was needed.
texts.3: SP conceived both the active and the potential hazards in the working area and regulated the flight parameters accordingly, adjusting the entry altitude before the conflicting traffic became a factor. The reasoning was passed to the wingman and to the IP as it was formed. The profile was preserved and every avoidance was unhurried.
texts.4: SP identified the potential hazards ahead of the flight, including a developing build-up and the recovery flow from the adjacent area, and regulated altitude, heading and speed in advance so that no avoidance manoeuvre was ever required. Contingency options were passed to the wingman before they were needed. Departures from the intended profile were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP conceived the hazards and regulated the parameters within standard, but the corrections were made once the hazard was already active rather than while it was still potential. The adjustments were therefore larger than the situation required. The standard was met; SP is expected to act on the potential hazard rather than wait for it to become present.

error_modes.label: Use of admissible clearing techniques for mid-air collision avoidance

texts.0: SP, due to an abbreviated and unbriefed clearing technique, did not use admissible clearing methods before the manoeuvre, omitting both the clearing turn and the check under the nose prior to the reversal. The airspace below and behind the formation was never covered and the IP took the aircraft to clear it before the manoeuvre could proceed. The correct sequence was reconstructed only in the debrief.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete application of the briefed clearing sequence, did not use the full admissible technique, cutting the clearing turn short and omitting the check under the nose before the descent. The complete sequence was flown only after the IP called for it, and the manoeuvre entry was delayed accordingly. SP retained control of the aircraft throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to the compressed timeline after the rejoin, started the manoeuvre entry with the clearing turn flown at less than the required displacement, but recognized the shortfall and repeated the clearing sequence in full before proceeding. The airspace was cleared before any energy was committed. The correction was self-initiated and timely.
texts.3: SP used admissible clearing techniques throughout, flying the clearing turns to the required displacement and checking under the nose and behind the formation before each manoeuvre. The sequence was applied consistently from the first manoeuvre to the last. No omission was identified.
texts.4: SP applied the clearing techniques with full coverage and no wasted time, adapting the pattern to the sun position and to the terrain background so that the difficult sectors received the longest look. The sequence was integrated into the manoeuvre flow without disturbing the formation. Any shortfall was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP used admissible clearing techniques within standard, but the coverage was routine in shape and the check under the nose was brief on the later manoeuvres. The technique held up while workload was low and thinned as it rose. The standard was met; SP is expected to hold the same coverage across the whole sortie.

error_modes.label: Use of R/T to create safe separation from air traffic

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not use the R/T to create safe separation from the air traffic, and the position report gave neither the formation's level nor its intentions. No traffic information was issued in response and the IP had to transmit and obtain the separation instruction. Separation was established by the IP rather than by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to an unstandard read-back that did not confirm the actual clearance, did not use the R/T effectively to separate the formation from the reported traffic, and the request for a level change was made too late to be useful. The correct call was made only after the IP prompted it twice, by which time the separation available was the minimum acceptable. SP kept the aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to phraseology that did not identify the formation as a flight, did not obtain the required traffic information at the first call, but recognized the ambiguity and re-transmitted with the correct call sign and intentions. The traffic was passed in time and separation was arranged without any manoeuvre. The correction was made without prompting.
texts.3: SP used the R/T effectively to create safe separation, reporting position, level and intentions in standard phraseology and requesting traffic information before entering the confined sectors. Read-backs were complete and accurate. No transmission required clarification.
texts.4: SP used the R/T to shape the traffic picture in advance, coordinating the formation's area entry and recovery so that separation existed before it ever had to be manoeuvred for. Transmissions were concise, standard and correctly timed against the frequency loading. Any deviation from standard phraseology was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP's R/T met the standard and produced the required separation, but transmissions were long and on two occasions were made while another station was replying. The intention was conveyed correctly each time, though not always on the first call. The standard was met; SP is expected to shorten the calls and improve frequency discipline.

error_modes.label: Position-dependent clearing as Wingman, towards the Leader in fingertip

texts.0: SP, due to a lookout habit carried over from the lead position, did not execute clearing according to his/her position within the formation and in fingertip cleared away from the Leader instead of towards him/her. The sector across the formation was left uncovered for the whole leg and the IP took the aircraft to clear it before the turn. The clearing responsibility for the position was not applied at any point of the leg.
texts.1: SP, due to attention consumed by holding the fingertip position, cleared only intermittently and did not consistently clear towards the Leader as the position requires. The correct clearing responsibility was applied only after the IP stated it on the intercom, and the coverage remained thin through the following turn. No control input by the IP was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to the increased station-keeping workload after the position change, initially cleared the sector appropriate to the previous position, but identified the error and resumed clearing towards the Leader within the same leg. The uncovered period was short and no traffic was a factor. The correction was self-initiated.
texts.3: SP executed clearing appropriate to his/her position within the formation, clearing towards the Leader in fingertip and shifting the coverage correctly at each position change. Station keeping was maintained while the lookout was carried out. The sector split was applied consistently.
texts.4: SP executed position-dependent clearing without any gap through route, fingertip and echelon, adjusting the coverage immediately on each position change and calling detected traffic with accurate relative position. Formation position was held throughout the lookout. Any shortfall in coverage was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP cleared towards the Leader as the fingertip position requires and met the standard, but the looks away from the Leader were short and were often traded for station keeping when the formation manoeuvred. Coverage was adequate in level flight and thinned in the turns. The standard was met; SP is expected to sustain the clearing scan through manoeuvring.

error_modes.label: Wingman monitoring of radio transmissions and explicit perception of the situation

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the formation's position in the recovery, did not monitor the radio transmissions and had no explicit perception of the situation, missing both the frequency change and the traffic passed to the flight. The aircraft was left on the previous frequency until the IP transmitted and reset it. SP was unable to state the flight's clearance when asked.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness after the unplanned change of sequence, monitored the transmissions only partially and could not state the traffic that had been passed to the formation. The picture was rebuilt only after the IP recapitulated the clearance on the intercom, and the delay left SP behind the flight through the next leg. Control of the aircraft was retained by SP.
texts.2: SP, due to situational awareness limited to the instrument in use during the fuel check, missed one transmission made to the formation, but recognized the gap and requested confirmation from the Leader without prompting. The picture was restored before the recovery point. No IP action was required.
texts.3: SP monitored the radio transmissions throughout and held an explicit perception of the situation, being able to state the formation's clearance, the reported traffic and the next expected event at any time. Frequency changes were followed without prompting. The picture was maintained through the busy phases.
texts.4: SP monitored all transmissions and maintained an explicit and forward-looking perception of the situation, anticipating the recovery instructions and having the next frequency and the traffic picture ready before they were required. The awareness was shared with the Leader in short accurate calls. Any lapse in monitoring was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the transmissions and held an adequate picture of the situation, meeting the standard, but on two occasions the picture was rebuilt by asking the Leader rather than by continuous listening. Awareness lagged the flight slightly during the recovery. The standard was met; SP is expected to keep the picture current from the monitoring itself.

error_modes.label: Division of attention inside and outside the cockpit against mid-air and CFIT

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single caution indication at the expense of the outside scan, did not divide attention appropriately between the work inside and outside the cockpit, and neither the airspace nor the terrain clearance was monitored during the low segment. The descent was continued towards rising ground until the IP took the aircraft and climbed the formation. The division of attention was not restored on SP's own initiative.
texts.1: SP, due to absorption in a cockpit indication that left the descent rate unmonitored, did not divide attention appropriately between the visual and R/T stimuli and the flight path, and terrain clearance reduced steadily through the turn. The scan was restored only after the IP called the altitude twice, and the recovery to the briefed floor was late. SP kept control of the aircraft.
texts.2: SP, due to attention captured by a minor system indication while the aircraft state went unmonitored, allowed the outside scan to lapse during the working phase, but detected the altitude drift and re-established the inside and outside division without prompting. Terrain and traffic margins were preserved throughout. The correction was made early.
texts.3: SP divided attention appropriately between the work inside and outside the cockpit, handling the visual and R/T stimuli without leaving either the airspace or the terrain clearance unmonitored. Cockpit tasks were deferred or shed when the workload rose. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP distributed attention between cockpit tasks, the R/T and the outside scan with clear priority to collision and terrain avoidance, sequencing the inside work into the low-workload segments so that neither hazard was ever unmonitored. The sequencing was deliberate and had been briefed. Any imbalance was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP divided attention within standard, but the inside-cockpit blocks were long enough that the outside scan was carried in short bursts during the busiest part of the working phase. Both hazards remained monitored, though with less margin than the technique allows. The standard was met; SP is expected to break the cockpit tasks into shorter blocks.

error_modes.label: Sectored visual scan with 20-30 degree arcs and refocus after instrument crosscheck

texts.0: SP, due to a sweeping scan that never settled into arcs of approximately 20-30 degrees and to a failure to refocus on a distant point after each instrument crosscheck, kept the eyes at the natural focus distance of about 18 inches for most of the transit to the working area. Traffic converging from the left front went undetected until the IP called it and took the aircraft to open the flight path. No cloud or ground reference was used as a focus point inside any arc.
texts.1: SP, due to arcs swept far wider than the 20-30 degrees the technique calls for and to dwell times well under the 3-5 seconds required, did not give the eyes time to acquire distant contacts and did not refocus outside after the fuel and engine crosscheck. The scan was rebuilt arc by arc only after two verbal prompts from the IP on the same leg. Separation from the reported traffic stayed at the minimum acceptable margin and no control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a fast continuous sweep resumed straight out of a head-down radio setup, lost the sectored pattern for one leg and looked through the airspace rather than into it. SP recognized the loss of the pattern, refocused on a distant cloud and rebuilt the search in 20-30 degree arcs with a 3-5 second dwell before the next turn. The correction was unprompted and no separation issue developed.
texts.3: SP searched the airspace in arcs of approximately 20-30 degrees and focused on a distant point within each arc for 3-5 seconds, refocusing outside after every instrument crosscheck. Contacts were acquired at a range that allowed unhurried heading adjustment. The scanning technique was held through both the area work and the recovery.
texts.4: SP held a disciplined sectored scan throughout, using distant cloud and ground references inside each 20-30 degree arc and refocusing outside immediately after each crosscheck so that no period was flown with the eyes settled at the natural 18 inch focus. Distant traffic was acquired well before it became a factor and passed to the wingman with accurate relative motion. Departures from the prescribed scanning technique were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP scanned in arcs and refocused outside within standard, but the dwell inside each arc drifted toward the short end and the arcs widened as cockpit tasks increased. The technique held over the front quadrant and thinned over the rear sectors. The standard was met on this sortie; SP is expected to hold the 3-5 second dwell and keep the arc width constant when task loading rises.

error_modes.label: Detection of a constant bearing contact using heading changes and wing flash

texts.0: SP, due to accepting a contact that stayed motionless against the canopy as a distant target of no consequence, did not recognize the constant relative bearing and made no slight heading change to create the relative movement required for detection. The aircraft was in fact on a collision course and the IP took control and turned the formation clear of the flight path. No wing flash or rock was attempted even after the traffic had been called on the radio.
texts.1: SP, due to a target held on a constant bearing and therefore appearing stationary in the canopy, did not initiate the small heading change that would have produced relative movement and continued to search the same sector without result. The heading offset was flown only after the IP directed it, and the resulting flight path passed close to the 500 foot minimum. Control of the aircraft remained with SP throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a converging contact that showed no movement against the canopy, was slow to interpret the constant bearing as a collision geometry, but recognized the cue without prompting and flew a slight heading change that immediately produced the relative motion needed. Once the target was acquired, the intended flight path was opened well beyond the 500 foot minimum. The correction was early and required no abrupt manoeuvring.
texts.3: SP recognized that a contact holding a constant relative bearing is difficult to see because it appears stationary in the canopy and used a slight heading change to create the relative movement required for detection. The target was acquired and the intended flight path was kept well clear of it. No prompting by the IP was necessary.
texts.4: SP interpreted the constant bearing cue at long range, generated the relative movement with a minimal heading change, and used a wing flash when the wingman reported the traffic close but not visually acquired. The flight path was kept far outside the 500 foot minimum with no disruption to the profile. Any shortfall in the technique was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP used heading changes to break out contacts on a constant bearing within standard, but the technique was applied only after each target had been searched for over an extended period. Acquisition therefore came at a range that left less room than intended. The standard was met; SP is expected to apply the heading change as soon as a constant bearing is suspected rather than after a prolonged search.

error_modes.label: Canopy bow restrictions and clearing turns for the blind areas beneath the aircraft

texts.0: SP, due to no allowance for the restrictions to visibility created by the canopy bows and no clearing turn before entering the manoeuvring block, left the areas beneath the fuselage and wings unchecked inside the training area. Traffic masked by the forward bow was called by the IP, who took the aircraft to clear the flight path. No high bank turn or turn of approximately 90 degrees off the established heading was flown at any point.
texts.1: SP, due to a fixed head position that left the canopy bow sectors permanently masked, did not clear beneath the aircraft before the area work, and the clearing turns were flown only after the IP directed them. The turns that resulted were shallow and fell well short of the approximately 90 degrees off the established heading needed to expose the blind areas. Separation was preserved but at the lower limit of what was acceptable.
texts.2: SP, due to head movement too small to look around the canopy bows, initially cleared only the sectors visible from the seated position and started the area work with the underside unchecked. SP recognized the omission, moved the head to unmask the bow sectors and flew a high bank clearing turn before continuing. The self-correction was made without prompting and no conflict developed.
texts.3: SP allowed for the visibility restrictions created by the canopy bows by moving the head to unmask those sectors, and used clearing turns of approximately 90 degrees off the established heading to clear the blind areas beneath the fuselage and wings before manoeuvring. Each block of work was entered with the airspace confirmed clear. No intervention by the IP was required.
texts.4: SP treated the canopy bow sectors as areas requiring deliberate unmasking and cleared the space beneath the fuselage and wings with well judged high bank clearing turns before every entry into the block. The turns were positioned so that they also exposed the airspace the formation was about to occupy, at no cost to the profile. Deviations from the required coverage were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for the canopy bows and flew clearing turns within standard, but the turns were consistently short of the magnitude needed to fully expose the areas beneath the aircraft. Coverage was adequate early in the sortie and became more perfunctory as it progressed. The standard was met; SP is expected to fly the clearing turn to full magnitude regardless of profile pressure.

error_modes.label: Clearing on the radios at pattern choke points without channelizing on reported positions

texts.0: SP, due to channelizing on the position information passed over the radio instead of prioritizing it against what could be seen, narrowed the search to a single quadrant and treated the call as a complete traffic picture. Mandatory transmissions at the known pattern choke points were missed, so the formation arrived at initial without a position report. The IP made the calls and directed the deconfliction.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting radio position information at face value without allowing for the varying accuracy of that information, searched only the quadrant that had been called and did not clear on the radios at the pattern choke points on his/her own initiative. The mandatory transmissions were made only after the IP prompted each one in turn. Pattern separation remained acceptable but at the lower limit.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on a radio position report while entering the pattern, was late with the mandatory transmission for the choke point ahead and initially searched only the quadrant that had been called. SP reprioritized without prompting, made the call and widened the visual search to the adjacent sectors before the turn. Pattern deconfliction was never in question.
texts.3: SP used position reports and radio position information to narrow the visual clearing to the likely quadrants while continuing to search the remaining sectors, and complied with the mandatory transmissions at each choke point. Knowledge of the local traffic flow was applied to anticipate where conflicts were most likely. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP integrated radio derived traffic information with a full visual search, weighing each reported position against the variable accuracy of that information, and cleared on the radios at every choke point with correct and timely transmissions. The traffic picture was passed to the wingman in enough detail for independent acquisition. Any shortfall was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP cleared on the radios and complied with the mandatory transmissions within standard, but the visual search increasingly went only where the radio pointed. The remaining quadrants received progressively less coverage as the pattern work continued. The standard was met; SP is expected to treat radio information as a cue that narrows the search rather than one that replaces it.

error_modes.label: Priority order of clearing against the other Number 1 and Number 2 responsibilities
error_modes.source: technique:9.3 RESPONSIBILITIES - FLIGHT LEADER, NUMBER 1 AND NUMBER 2

texts.0: SP, as Number 1, due to working navigation and communication tasks ahead of the higher priority of clearing for the formation, left the airspace ahead of the flight unchecked while reprogramming the route. Monitoring of Number 2 stopped over the same period, so neither the formation nor the wingman was being cleared for. The IP took the aircraft, cleared the sector and directed the flight back onto the briefed track.
texts.1: SP, as Number 2, due to backing up Number 1 on navigation and frequency management at the expense of the higher priorities, allowed clearing for the formation to degrade and did not reprioritize on his/her own initiative. The IP had to call for the reprioritization in the order taught before the outside scan was restored. Position and visual contact on Number 1 were held throughout and no control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a lower priority task taken up while the formation was repositioning, let clearing for the formation slip behind backing up Number 1 for a short period. SP recognized that clearing was being degraded and reprioritized in the correct order without prompting, restoring the outside scan before the next turn. Flight path deconfliction and position were never affected.
texts.3: SP held the taught priority order, clearing for the formation ahead of planning, monitoring the wingman, navigation and communication as Number 1, and keeping deconfliction, visual contact and position ahead of clearing and backing up lead as Number 2. Lower priority tasks were deferred rather than allowed to erode the higher ones. No direction from the IP was needed at any stage.
texts.4: SP worked the priority order so cleanly that clearing for the formation was never interrupted, with navigation and radio work absorbed into natural gaps and the wingman monitored continuously. Whenever backing up Number 1 began to compete with clearing, the lower priority task was dropped at once and picked up later. Departures from the taught priority order were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept clearing ahead of the lower priority tasks within standard, but the margin was thin whenever backing up Number 1 and radio work arrived together. Clearing was preserved by shortening the scan rather than by deferring the lower priority task. The standard was met; SP is expected to shed the lower priority task instead of compressing the clearing scan.

error_modes.label: Blind call and lost sight procedures including the sun-blind case

texts.0: SP, due to treating a sun-blind condition as a momentary loss rather than an actual lost-sight case, did not make an immediate blind call with the current altitude and continued to manoeuvre towards the last known position of the other aircraft. Neither altitude nor heading was altered to open the geometry. The IP transmitted the blind call and directed the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over whether the loss of visual contact was genuine, delayed the blind call and then transmitted it without the current altitude, so no useful acknowledgement or deconfliction could follow. The complete call and the manoeuvre away from the last known position were made only after the IP directed both. Separation ended near the minimum acceptable and control of the aircraft remained with SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a sun-blind condition through the turn, was slow to classify the loss of visual contact as an actual lost-sight case, but made the blind call with the current altitude on his/her own initiative and altered altitude away from the last known position. Visual contact was regained shortly afterwards and the visual call was passed and acknowledged. No direction from the IP was required.
texts.3: SP treated every loss of visual contact, sun-blind periods included, as an actual lost-sight case and made an immediate blind call with the current altitude, adding turn direction and heading where appropriate. With no timely acknowledgement, SP manoeuvred away from the last known position and altered altitude, then rejoined no closer than route until the visual call was acknowledged. Deconfliction was assured throughout.
texts.4: SP called blind immediately and completely, with call sign, current altitude and turn information, and manoeuvred away from the last known position of the other aircraft as the call was made. When it became clear that both aircraft were blind, at least 1000 feet of altitude separation was established before any attempt to regain visual contact. The relative position transmitted by the other aircraft was used to talk the eyes back on, and deviations from the procedure were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP applied the lost sight procedure within standard, but each blind call was preceded by a short period of hesitation while SP searched for the other aircraft. On one occasion the altitude was added only after the initial transmission. The standard was met; SP is expected to call blind at once and continue the search afterwards.

error_modes.label: Route position used for clearing and stabilization before head-down tasks

texts.0: SP, due to starting the radio channel change and the in-flight checks before stabilizing in route, went head-down from a position still closing inside two ship widths and stopped clearing for the formation altogether. The spacing continued to reduce while the head was in the cockpit and the IP took the aircraft to re-establish route spacing. The automatic move to route for the channel change had not been made.
texts.1: SP, due to diverting attention to the in-flight checks before the route position was stable, let the spacing wander well inside the two to four ship widths used for cockpit tasks and made no attempt to move out towards the 500 foot limit that enhances clearing. The IP had to call for the position to be stabilized before the checks were resumed. Visual contact with Number 1 was retained and no control input by the IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an early start on the frequency change, began the head-down work before route was fully stabilized and lost the outside scan for a short period. SP recognized the sequence error, returned the attention outside, stabilized at about three ship widths and only then completed the change. Clearing for the formation was restored without prompting.
texts.3: SP moved to route automatically for the radio channel change and stabilized at two to four ship widths before diverting attention into the cockpit, returning outside between tasks. The wider spacing was used as intended to enhance the visual lookout for the formation. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP used route deliberately as a clearing position, flying line abreast out towards the 500 foot limit where the profile allowed and stabilizing before every head-down task. Cockpit work was broken into short blocks with the scan re-established between them, and the position never drifted forward of the extended 3/9 line or aft of the extended fingertip reference line. Any shortfall in technique was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP stabilized in route before the cockpit tasks within standard, but the spacing was consistently held at the inner edge of route, which limited the clearing benefit the position is flown for. The head-down blocks also lengthened as the checks progressed. The standard was met; SP is expected to move out towards the wider limit and keep the head-down blocks short.

error_modes.label: Mutual visual monitoring in fighting wing and extended trail

texts.0: SP, as Number 2, due to no continuous analysis of aspect angle and closure rate while manoeuvring, stagnated in Number 1's high 6 o'clock, where Number 1 cannot monitor the wingman, and the mutual visual was lost. No lead or lag pursuit correction was applied to re-establish the 30 to 45 degree cone and no terminate call was made. The IP directed the terminate and repositioned the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to pursuit selection that did not keep pace with the changing aspect angle, drifted repeatedly into Number 1's low 6 o'clock, outside the 4-5 and 7-8 o'clock sectors where Number 1 looks for the wingman behind the wing. The cone was regained only after the IP called for the correction on each occasion. Range stayed within limits and control of the aircraft remained with SP.
texts.2: SP, due to a late assessment of closure rate through the reversal, allowed the position to move towards the 6 o'clock where monitoring by Number 1 becomes difficult, but recognized the drift and applied lag pursuit to return into the 30 to 45 degree cone. The correction was made without prompting and the mutual visual was never lost. Range remained between 500 and 1000 feet aft of Number 1.
texts.3: SP maintained the fighting wing cone through continuous analysis of aspect angle and closure rate, staying in the sector behind the wing where Number 1 looks for the wingman rather than stagnating in the 6 o'clock. As Number 1, SP monitored the wingman's aspect, range, closure, heading crossing angle and line of sight throughout. No intervention by the IP was required.
texts.4: SP held the cone with early and minimal pursuit corrections so that the wingman remained continuously visible to Number 1 behind the wing, and passed a terminate call without hesitation when the geometry began to develop beyond what could be monitored. As Number 1, SP kept the manoeuvring smooth and predictable so that mutual visual and clearing for the formation were preserved. Departures from the cone parameters were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the cone and preserved the mutual visual within standard, but the position drifted towards the aft sector each time the manoeuvring became more dynamic. Corrections were made once the drift was established rather than anticipated. The standard was met; SP is expected to anticipate the aspect change and correct before the position approaches the 6 o'clock.
